_readme: Curated seed list of U.S. Supreme Court dockets. Selection rule (cases-seed-2): dockets a maintainer identified as election-law matters. Every place link quotes a passage from a named document of the docket; the pipeline checks on every run that the passage is in that document (ignoring line breaks, hyphenation and letter case) and that it names the place, and publishes the link only if both hold. 'evidence' is 'qp' (the Court's Questions Presented document), 'initiating' (first document linked from the docket) or 'opinion' (the opinion linked from the latest entry that links one); 'evidenceUrl' names a document linked from the docket instead, and 'evidenceLabel' says in words what that document is. Use […] inside a quote for words left out. 'tags' adds a subject tag the keyword rules miss, with a passage checked the same way. Notes are the maintainer's description and are not checked by machine. Choosing a passage: prefer the Court's own text (a per curiam opinion, an order or the opinion of the Court) or, where it does not name the place, a sentence that describes the facts, such as what a law provides or what a court held. Never use as a link's evidence a sentence in which a Justice or a party characterises another Justice's or another party's position or argument (for example a concurrence describing what the dissent would do, or one side's account of the other side's case), and avoid argumentative wording where a descriptive sentence in the same document names the place. Apply party labels symmetrically: a passage for a partisan-gerrymandering case names the political party that drew or benefited from a map only if the passages of every such case do; at present none does. When a passage comes from a separate opinion, 'evidenceLabel' says so.

geographies.note: Louisiana's congressional districting plan enacted as S.B. 8 (2024). The map shows the boundaries in the Census files, which may differ from the plan at issue.

geographies.quote: 1. Does Arizona's out-of-precinct policy violate Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act? 2. Does Arizona's ballot-collection law violate Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act or the Fifteenth Amendment?

geographies.note: Arizona's in-precinct voting requirement and limits on third-party ballot collection.
geographies.quote: the Ninth Circuit held that Arizona violated § 2 by (1) requiring in-person voters to cast ballots in their assigned precincts; and (2) prohibiting "ballot-harvesting," i.e., third-party collection and return of ballots.

tags.quote: Arizona gives all citizens an equal opportunity to vote in person or by mail, and authorizes ballots to be turned in by a family member, household member, or caregiver.

geographies.note: Mississippi law allowing mail-in absentee ballots to be received within five business days after election day.
geographies.quote: Mississippi allows some of those timely cast ballots (mail-in absentee ballots, in Mississippi's case) to be counted if they are received by election officials a short time after election day (in Mississippi, within 5 business days after election day).

geographies.note: Arizona voter-registration provisions on documentary proof of citizenship.
geographies.quote: Since 2004, Arizona has required newly registered voters to provide documentary proof of citizenship.

geographies.note: Pennsylvania's deadline for receiving mail-in ballots in the 2020 general election. In the sentences left out of the passage, the dissent says that the Pennsylvania Democratic Party sued in state court and argued that the court could extend the deadline under the clause of the State Constitution providing that elections shall be “free and equal” (art. I, § 5); that is the argument the state court agreed with.
geographies.quote: in October 2019, the Pennsylvania Legislature overhauled its election laws. Relevant here, it gave all voters the option of voting by mail, and it extended the deadline for officials to receive mail ballots by several days to 8 p.m. on election day. […] The Pennsylvania Supreme Court agreed. On September 17, it held that this “free and equal” provision enabled the court to extend the deadline three days to accommodate concerns about postal delays.
